paper_title: Scaling to Tens of Thousands of Test-Time Iterations with Loop-Native Attention Residuals

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: In this paper, we argue that looped Transformers need their own residual connections to prevent performance degradation as the number of iterations grows. We observe that increasing loop iterations can reduce reasoning accuracy: noisy state updates overwrite correct intermediate deductions and even undo completed solutions. This leaves subsequent iterations to recover lost information from an already degraded representation: once an error arises in an earlier loop, often as a result of long-range propagation through the recurrence, later loops find it difficult to correct. In this paper, we introduce InfiLoop, a loop-native residual connection that learns which past computations to retain and how much to accept from each new update. InfiLoop combines content-based weighting with learned temporal decay to maintain a running summary of recurrent states. An exact streaming recurrence keeps its persistent aggregation memory constant as the loop count grows. The resulting adaptive update suppresses unreliable proposals and preserves useful intermediate states. Across extensive reasoning tasks, a 7M-parameter InfiLoop model outperforms existing recursive architectures, reaching 97.9% exact accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme, and 13.6% pass@2 on ARC-AGI-2. Notably, on Sudoku-Extreme, InfiLoop continues to improve with test-time looping beyond 20,000 effective steps, showing that added depth translates directly into stronger reasoning. Our code is available at https://github.com/pixeli99/InfiLoop.

sections.content: Scaling to Tens of Thousands of Test-Time Iterations with Loop-Native Attention Residuals Pengxiang Li1, Dilxat Muhtar2, Di He3,4,5, Guinan Su6,7,8, Lu Yin9, Shiwei Liu6,7,8, 1The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, 2Independent Researcher, 3Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, 4Peng Cheng Laboratory, 5University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, 6ELLIS Institute Tubingen, 7Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, 8Tubingen AI Center, 9Shenzhen University of Advanced Technology Corresponding author: sliu@tue.ellis.eu In this paper, we argue that looped Transformers need their own residual connections to prevent performance degradation as the number of iterations grows. We observe that increasing loop iterations can reduce reasoning accuracy: noisy state updates overwrite correct intermediate deductions and even undo completed solutions. This leaves subsequent iterations to recover lost information from an already degraded representation: once an error arises in an earlier loop, often as result of long-range propagation through the recurrence, later loops find it difficult to correct. In this paper, we introduce InfiLoop, loop-native residual connection that learns which past computations to retain and how much to accept from each new update. InfiLoop combines content-based weighting with learned temporal decay to maintain running summary of recurrent states. An exact streaming recurrence keeps its persistent aggregation memory constant as the loop count grows. The resulting adaptive update suppresses unreliable proposals and preserves useful intermediate states. Across extensive reasoning tasks, 7M-parameter InfiLoop model outperforms existing recursive architectures, reaching 97.9% exact accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme, and 13.6% pass@2 on ARC-AGI-2. Notably, on Sudoku-Extreme, InfiLoop continues to improve with test-time looping beyond 20,000 effective steps, showing that added depth translates directly into stronger reasoning. Our code is available at https://github.com/pixeli99/InfiLoop. 1. Introduction Looped Transformers address complex reasoning tasks by repeatedly applying shared Transformer block (Dehghani et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2025; Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025). Each iteration adds another sequence of layer transformations, increasing computational depth without introducing additional parameters. This allows models to devote more computation to reasoning by executing more loops at test time (Saunshi et al., 2025; Geiping et al., 2025). common way to connect consecutive iterations is to feed the final output of one loop directly into the next, strategy we refer to as the carry-last rule. Although effective, this rule makes the unrolled computation equivalent to deep network with weights shared across repeated blocks. Increasing the loop count therefore returns us to familiar question: does adding more depth lead to more useful computation? Standard deep Transformers suffer from the curse of depth (Sun et al., 2025), where the contribution of deeper layers progressively diminishes. Repeatedly applying shared block can compound this limitation, as the same transformations are applied at every iteration and the residual stream grows with the loop count. Related limitations have also been examined in fixed-point looping (Movahedi et al., 2026). Existing remedies use decay or layer scaling to control residual growth and regulate update magnitudes (Sun et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026; Movahedi et al., 2026). These interventions address how strongly each update affects the representation, but leave central architectural choice unchanged: the next loop still receives only the latest recurrent state. We argue that this state-replacement rule is key bottleneck in deep looped transformers. Under carry-last, earlier computations remain accessible only through the information preserved in the latest state. Standard Pre-LN or Post-LN 1 Loop-Native Attention Residuals Figure 1. Carry-last keeps changing its state after solving and loses solutions. (a) Exact accuracy against effective depth, the number of executed Transformer layers, on Sudoku-Extreme. Each outer update executes 26 layers. TRM peaks at 468 layers and then loses accuracy as depth grows. (b) Relative state change after the update at which each model first solves puzzle, for the puzzles that both models solve within 36 updates. TRM settles briefly and then moves its state again. (c) Share of those puzzles whose solution is still correct. residual connections provide paths for this information to propagate, but do not explicitly retain and select among outputs from earlier loops. Consequently, noisy or undesirable iteration can degrade useful representations throughout propagation, leading to sub-optimal performance, as shown in Figure 1. This motivates changing how information is combined across loops, so that further computation can build on useful intermediate states without relying exclusively on the most recent output. To this end, we introduce InfiLoop, loop-native residual connection that replaces the carry-last rule with learned attention over recurrent outputs. shared pseudo-query scores each candidate when it is produced, while learned exponential decay discounts earlier contributions. The resulting normalized aggregation forms the input to the next iteration. Crucially, shared scoring and geometric decay admit an exact streaming recurrence, requiring only weighted-state vector and normalization scalar per token, with persistent aggregation memory independent of the loop count. This recurrence is equivalent to an adaptive residual update that balances the accumulated state against each new candidate, allowing the model to regulate how strongly subsequent computations alter its reasoning state. This paper establishes four findings. First, empirical diagnosis reveals that carry-last destabilizes solved states at large depth, while InfiLoop preserves solutions indefinitely. Second, the exact recurrence guarantees constant-memory state combination across arbitrarily long reasoning trajectories. Third, on extensive reasoning benchmarks, InfiLoop surpasses strong damping baselines while requiring substantially fewer layer evaluations. Fourth, inspection of the learned step size reveals an emergent self-verification behavior: the connection discounts outputs produced during unsolved search, accepts the output that completes the solution, and freezes the state once solved. 2. Deeper Loops Undo Earlier Progress We measure where looped reasoner breaks as depth grows. On Sudoku-Extreme, we compare InfiLoop with the selfattention TRM, carry-last model. Both checkpoints are trained with the same loop schedule, and we run both for 72 outer updates. After each outer update, we decode the predicted board and measure the relative change of the outer state, ht ht1/ht1. We average this change over initially empty cells. Figure 1 plots exact accuracy against effective depth, the number of executed Transformer layers, and tracks the state change after solving. 2 Loop-Native Attention Residuals Figure 2. Connecting successive applications of shared block. (a) TRM uses the carry-last rule: the candidate zt becomes the next recurrent state, ht = zt. (b) InfiLoop combines earlier candidates into the state ht passed to the next block application, using content weights and exponential temporal decay. Colors identify candidates from different iterations; the illustrated contributions are schematic. The same block parameters are reused at every recurrent step. Accuracy peaks and then falls with depth. TRM reaches its best exact accuracy of 62.2% at 468 layers, but its accuracy declines to 58.1% at 1,872 layers. InfiLoop keeps improving over the same depth and reaches 90.9%. The predictions show the same pattern. During updates 36 to 72, TRM changes 77.0 predictions per puzzle on initially empty cells, and its number of incorrect cells rises by 0.21 per puzzle. Repeated changes to the same cell count separately. Over the same window, InfiLoop makes 24.0 changes and removes 1.25 incorrect cells per puzzle. Correct intermediate predictions are lost. TRM overwrites correct predictions in later updates. At update 36, both models predict 1.42 million initially empty cells correctly. During the remaining updates, TRM turns 20.9% of these predictions into an incorrect value at least once, and InfiLoop turns 2.4% of them. The right two panels of Figure 1 align each puzzle to its first solving update. Within 5 updates after solving, TRM reduces its state change to 3% of the state norm, but the change then climbs back to 10% per update and stays there. TRM begins to lose solutions after 9 updates and has lost 19.7% of them after 36 updates. The state change of InfiLoop instead falls to 0.3% per update, and every puzzle solved by InfiLoop remains solved 36 updates later. Learning what to carry forward. newer output is not necessarily better output, yet carry-last passes every new block output to the next iteration in full. Earlier outputs reach later iterations only through the newest output, so the connection between iterations decides what the loop keeps. We therefore replace carry-last with learned residual connection. running summary holds the contributions of earlier outputs, and the connection learns how much of each new output to add to it. The summary becomes the input to the next iteration, so the learned connection acts during reasoning and not on predictions after reasoning ends. shared scorer weights each output once, at its own iteration, and learned decay reduces the contributions of older outputs. The weighted summary has an exact recurrent form, and its persistent memory does not grow with the number of iterations. Section 3 defines the connection and derives its recurrence. 3. Exact Recurrence with Constant Memory Directly evaluating the sums in Equation 3 would require retaining the full candidate history. The shared scorer and exponential temporal decay make this unnecessary: historical content scores remain unchanged, and their weights decay by the same factor at each step. Specifically, let ei = exp(si) and β = eλ (0, 1), so that exp(si λ(t i)) = eiβti. Separating the newest contribution gives Nt = Dt = t1 (cid:88) i=0 t1 (cid:88) i=0 βtieizi + etzt = βNt1 + etzt, βtiei + et = βDt1 + et. (4) We initialize N0 = e0z0 and D0 = e0, which yields h0 = z0, and recover the state at each step as ht = Nt/Dt. The recurrence is algebraically identical to Equation 2; no approximation to the attention weights is introduced. 3.3. (5) The attention aggregation thus implements an adaptive step toward the new candidate. The step size γt compares the candidates content weight et with the retained historical mass βDt1. When et βDt1, γt approaches one and the new candidate dominates. When et βDt1, γt approaches zero and the previous state is largely preserved. The learned scorer can therefore suppress low-scoring proposals while accepting high-scoring ones. Because the attention weights are positive and sum to one, ht lies in the convex hull of the candidate states, i.e., ht max0it zi. Thus, aggregation does not amplify the norm beyond that of the largest candidate. uniform bound over arbitrarily many iterations additionally requires the candidate norms to remain bounded. Moreover, our framework applies to both standard looped Transformers (Dehghani et al., 2019) and nested recurrent reasoners like TRM (Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025) and HRM (Wang et al., 2025). For standard looped Transformer, we replace the carry-last assignment with Equation 4. For nested looped architectures, we apply the same rule independently to each recurrent axis. The inner and outer states each have separate scorerdecay pair (q, β) and accumulators (N, D), adding + 1 learned parameters per axis while keeping the aggregation state independent of the loop count. 4 Loop-Native Attention Residuals 3.4. Computational and Memory Complexity Our aggregation stores only vector Nt Rd and scalar Dt per token, requiring O(d) persistent memory and O(d) computation per iteration. Over iterations, its total aggregation cost is O(T d), while its memory footprint remains independent of the loop count. In contrast, Full Attention Residuals with iteration-specific queries stores and attends over all preceding representations, requiring O(td) memory and computation at step (Kimi Team et al., 2026). Our recurrence therefore reduces peak persistent memory from O(T d) to O(d) and total aggregation cost from O(T 2d) to O(T d). 4. Experiments We evaluate InfiLoop against recursive and looped reasoning models across symbolic puzzle benchmarks and abstract visual transformation tasks. Our implementation builds upon the public TRM codebase (Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025) and adopts its deep-supervision training procedure. We first describe the benchmarks and evaluation protocol, then report complete system performance, examine test-time compute and depth scaling, and analyze the emergent verification dynamics of the learned connection. 4.1. Dataset description In the following, we provide structured description of each dataset used in this paper. We refer the reader to the cited literature for further information. Sudoku-Extreme. The task consists of exceptionally challenging, partially filled 9 9 Sudoku puzzles with unique solutions, introduced by Wang et al. (2025). Each board is flattened into sequence of length 81. The training set contains 1,000 unique base puzzles, each augmented 1,000 times through digit permutations and spatial symmetries, yielding approximately 1M training samples. The test data contains 422,786 unique puzzles. The evaluation metric is exact sequence accuracy, requiring all 81 board cells to match the ground truth. Maze-Hard. The task consists of 30 30 shortest-path maze puzzles, introduced by Wang et al. (2025). Each grid contains open navigable cells, impassable walls, an origin, and destination. The model predicts flattened grid marking the reference shortest path. The training and test sets each contain 1,000 unique samples. Following Wang et al. (2025), we apply no data augmentation to this task. The evaluation metric is exact sequence accuracy. ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2. The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus assesses whether reasoning system can induce an underlying transformation rule from minimal demonstrations (Chollet, 2019; Chollet et al., 2024). ARC-AGI-1 provides two or more demonstration pairs (typically three) of coloured 2D grids with variable dimensions up to 30 30, and requires generating the output grid for held-out test input. ARC-AGI-2 keeps this format while presenting substantially more intricate problems that compose multiple transformations and resist brute-force search (Chollet et al., 2025). ARC-AGI-1 has 400 public training tasks and 400 public evaluation tasks; ARC-AGI-2 has 1,000 public training tasks and 120 public evaluation tasks.1 The evaluation metric is pass@2 accuracy, selecting the top two candidate outputs aggregated across augmented test-time views. Pretrained reasoning language models with chain-of-thought struggle on both benchmarks: DeepSeek-R1 with 671B parameters attains 15.8% on ARC-AGI-1 and 1.3% on ARC-AGI-2, while Claude 3.7 Sonnet (16K) attains 28.6% and 0.7%, respectively, as reported in Table 1. 4.2. Evaluation protocol Model architecture. We evaluate compact 7M-parameter recursive reasoner that implements the nested looping architecture in Section 3.3. Its shared recursive block contains two Transformer layers with hidden dimension 512, eight attention heads, SwiGLU activations (Shazeer, 2020) with an expansion factor of four, and depthwise 3 3 convolution. Across both the inner and outer recurrent loops, the model replaces standard carry-last state replacement with our loop-native attention residual connection, parameterized by 513-parameter scorerdecay pair (q, β) per axis. Baselines. We benchmark InfiLoop against the primary looped reasoning paradigms: (1) TRM-Att (7M parameters) (Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025), the standard self-attention recursive reasoner using carry-last state propagation; (2) FPRM (7M parameters) (Movahedi et al., 2026), released looped model that stabilizes iterations via pre-norm, learned residual scaling, and damped fixed-point updates; (3) HRM (Wang et al., 2025), Attractor Models (Fein-Ashley & Rashidinejad, 1Official ARC-AGI-2 dataset: https://github.com/arcprize/ARC-AGI-2. 5 Loop-Native Attention Residuals Table 1. For direct controlled comparisons, we evaluate the official released checkpoint of FPRM on Sudoku-Extreme and retrain the TRM baseline with the authors published recipe. Training configuration. For Sudoku-Extreme, we train InfiLoop on 1,000 base puzzles with 1,000 augmentations per puzzle. We optimize using AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) with peak learning rate 104, weight decay 1.0, and batch size 768. The training schedule executes = 3 outer loops and = 6 inner updates across 12 deep-supervision segments. Each segment executes 21 shared-block applications, with gradients backpropagated through the final seven. For Maze-Hard and ARC benchmarks, training employs = 3, = 6 across up to 16 supervision segments with peak learning rate 3 104. Appendix provides complete hyperparameter and resource accounting. 4.3. Reasoning performance across puzzle benchmarks The complete InfiLoop reasoner achieves the highest performance among the 7M-parameter configurations listed in Table 1 across the four benchmarks. On Sudoku-Extreme, InfiLoop achieves 97.9% exact accuracy, surpassing FPRM at 94.2% and reported TRM-Att at 74.7%. On Maze-Hard, InfiLoop achieves 87.4% accuracy, exceeding both TRM-Att at 85.3% and FPRM at 87.0%. On ARC-AGI-1, InfiLoop reaches 49.1% pass@2, improving upon FPRM at 47.5% and TRM-Att at 44.6%. On the challenging ARC-AGI-2 benchmark, InfiLoop attains 13.6% pass@2, nearly doubling TRM-Att at 7.8% and outperforming FPRM at 6.2%. We also reproduce the TRM baseline ourselves, marked in Table 1. Retraining TRM on Sudoku-Extreme with the authors published recipe gives 73.6%, close to the 74.7% they report. Evaluating the released ARC-AGI-2 verification checkpoint under our protocol yields 4.6% pass@2. All baseline comparisons in the following sections use the retrained checkpoint. 4.4. Test-time depth and compute efficiency We next evaluate how InfiLoop translates recurrent computation into reasoning accuracy. We conduct controlled evaluations on fixed sample of Sudoku-Extreme test puzzles across varying layer budgets without retraining. With two Transformer layers per shared block, executing supervision segments, outer cycles, and inner updates corresponds to 2SH(L + 1) layer evaluations. Loop-Native Attention Residuals Figure 3. Test-time scaling and accuracy across puzzle difficulty. Left: Exact accuracy against executed Transformer layers (logarithmic axis), with all three models evaluated to 24,960 layers. InfiLoop reaches 90.9% at 1,872 layers, exceeding FPRMs 90.1% at 3,744 layers with half the layer evaluations. Right: Exact accuracy by empty-cell count at matched 1,872 layers. Comparison with FPRM under test-time scaling. Figure 3 (left) compares InfiLoop against the released FPRM checkpoint and retrained TRM across executed layers up to 24,960. At 1,872 layer evaluations, InfiLoop achieves 90.9% exact accuracy overall. This exceeds FPRMs 90.1% accuracy at 3,744 layer evaluations, cutting the required computation in half. When matched at 3,744 layer evaluations, InfiLoop reaches 92.4% overall, maintaining steady advantage over FPRM at 90.1%. Furthermore, the accuracy that InfiLoop achieves at 936 layer evaluations (86.5%) is never matched by TRM even when evaluated at 24,960 layers (83.65%), more than 26 times deeper. At 24,960 layer evaluations, exact accuracy is 92.74% for InfiLoop, 91.63% for FPRM, and 83.65% for TRM. Accuracy across puzzle difficulties. Figure 3 (right) evaluates accuracy as function of the number of empty cells in the input grid, an established proxy for Sudoku difficulty. We evaluate all difficulty levels from 45 to 60 empty cells on the 32,768 test puzzles at matched 1,872 layer evaluations. For easy puzzles with 45 to 51 empty cells, both InfiLoop and FPRM achieve 100.0% exact accuracy. From 52 empty cells onward, the margin of InfiLoop over FPRM stays between 1.5 and 6.2 percentage points, while the margin over TRM rises from 4.2 percentage points at 52 empty cells to 23.4 at 60. At 52 empty cells, InfiLoop attains 100.0% accuracy against 96.5% for FPRM (+3.5 percentage points) and 95.8% for TRM (+4.2 percentage points). At 55 empty cells, InfiLoop scores 93.4% against 90.3% for FPRM (+3.2 percentage points) and 84.2% for TRM (+9.3 percentage points). At 58 empty cells, the margin over FPRM peaks at +6.2 percentage points (84.1% versus 77.9%), while the margin over TRM widens to +19.6 percentage points. At the most difficult count of 60 empty cells, InfiLoop maintains 59.5% accuracy against 56.5% for FPRM (+3.0 percentage points) and 36.0% for TRM (+23.4 percentage points). Learned state reuse shields intermediate deductions precisely when search paths are deep and complex. 4.5. Because candidate states with constraint violations receive small content weights et, the recurrence limits the influence of noisy updates on the accumulated state. To test whether this mechanism stabilizes the trajectory against perturbations, we inject relative perturbation ϵ [104, 0.3] into the recurrent state at update 36 and unroll the model for another 36 updates. As shown in Figure 5a, InfiLoop retains 100% of its solved puzzles at update 72 across all tested perturbation scales, while TRM loses 1520% of solutions even without perturbation. Figure 5b tracks the relative Euclidean distance to the unperturbed trajectory over subsequent updates k. For TRM, even minimal perturbation of ϵ = 104 causes the trajectory to diverge to relative distance of order one within 12 updates. In contrast, InfiLoop keeps the displacement bounded throughout subsequent iterations, showing that the learned aggregation prevents chaotic drift in the recurrent state. 4.6. Connection placement and decay initialization We evaluate the design choices underlying InfiLoop: the placement of the learned connection across recurrent loops, and the initialization of the temporal decay β0. Table 2 summarizes both ablations on 7,680 puzzles sampled uniformly at random from the Sudoku-Extreme test set. Applying the connection to both axes. The nested reasoner maintains two distinct recurrent trajectories: an inner loop for iterative candidate refinement, and an outer loop for context updates. Table 2 compares applying InfiLoop to the inner loop alone, the outer loop alone, and both loops simultaneously. The dual-axis configuration achieves the highest accuracy across all evaluated budgets. At the training depth of H3 L6, dual-axis aggregation reaches 82.1% accuracy, compared with an inner connection alone at 72.6% and an outer connection alone at 75.1%. This margin widens as the reasoning budget expands to H32 L6, reaching 89.7% against 79.4% and 80.0%. Both recurrent trajectories benefit from learned state reuse. Forward decay over the loop trajectory. The decay β = eλ sets how fast older block outputs lose weight in the aggregated state. Forward decay uses β < 1, so older outputs weigh less. Uniform weights use β = 1, which is the Full Attention Residuals case λ = 0. Reverse decay uses β > 1, so older outputs weigh more. We first fix β during training for the two-axis model. Reverse decay with β = 1.82 solves only 2.0% of the puzzles at H3 L6. Uniform weights reach 38.4%, and forward decay with β = 0.55 reaches 74.0%. The gap grows with the budget: at H32 L6, forward decay reaches 77.9%, uniform weights reach 40.2%, and reverse decay stays at 2.0%. Learning β from β0 = 0.55 gives the best accuracy, 82.1% at H3 L6 and 89.7% at H32 L6. The initialization also matters: β0 = 0.10 reaches 66.3% and β0 = 0.90 reaches 63.3% at H3 L6. We therefore learn forward decay from β0 = 0.55 on all benchmarks. 5. Conclusion We discuss related work in Appendix B. In this paper, we identify state replacement under the carry-last rule as primary bottleneck in deep looped Transformers: repeatedly replacing the recurrent state with the latest block output overwrites correct intermediate deductions and destabilizes solved configurations. To address this, we introduce InfiLoop, loop-native 9 Loop-Native Attention Residuals residual connection that combines content-based pseudo-query scoring with exponential temporal decay across iterations. Its exact recurrence needs only O(d) persistent memory per token and keeps the aggregated state within the convex hull of the candidate representations. On Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, ARC-AGI-1, and ARC-AGI-2, InfiLoop outperforms carry-last and fixed-point damping baselines, and it reaches their accuracy with fewer layers under test-time depth scaling. Furthermore, analysis of the learned connection reveals that it operates as an adaptive residual update: the model suppresses proposals with constraint violations, increases update magnitude upon reaching valid solution, and resists state drift under perturbations. These findings show that learning how to selectively aggregate recurrent states is an effective mechanism for scaling test-time reasoning depth.

Compute and Persistent-State Accounting Loop-Native Attention Residuals We quantify the computation and persistent state of InfiLoop. It stores 582.8 KiB of persistent state per puzzle, independent of the loop budget. Layer evaluations. Each outer cycle applies the shared block times to the inner state and once to the outer state. With supervision segments, outer cycles per segment, and layers per block, the number of Transformer layer evaluations is C(H, L) = SH(L + 1)K. (6) Training uses S=12, H=3, L=6, and K=2, which gives 504 layer evaluations. The depth study in Section 4.4 fixes H=6 and L=12, so each segment executes 156 layers, and varies from 1 to 160, which gives 156 to 24,960 layer evaluations. This count omits the connection and the prediction heads, which we add below. The embedding is table lookup and adds no multiply-accumulates. FPRM also uses two-layer block with width 512 and the same sequence length. Layer evaluations therefore match the dominant Transformer arithmetic across the two models. FPRMs solver operations are outside the InfiLoop FLOP accounting below. These counts do not compare measured runtime. Profiling setup and FLOP convention. We profile the InfiLoop Sudoku checkpoint at batch size one under the 12-segment inference protocol. Each sequence has 81 board cells and 16 prefix positions, so the shared block processes n=97 positions. The SwiGLU intermediate width is m=1,536: the implementation takes two thirds of the expansion 4d and rounds it up to multiple of 256. We count two FLOPs per multiply-accumulate in linear projections, attention matrix products, the depthwise convolution, and the content scores of the connection. Normalization, activation functions, rotary embeddings (Su et al., 2024), other elementwise arithmetic, and data movement are not counted. Counted FLOPs. Let be the hidden width, the number of board cells, and kc the convolution kernel width. One application of the shared block costs Fblock = K(8nd2 + 4n2d + 6ndm) + 2gdk2 , (7) where the convolution applies once per block to the board cells and the attention and feed-forward projections apply to all positions. For n=97, d=512, m=1536, K=2, g=81, kc=3, this is 1.36154 GFLOPs per block application in InfiLoop. The prediction head has =11 outputs per position. The halting head of the adaptive computation procedure has two outputs and reads one position. With =SH(L + 1) block applications, the counted total is FInfiLoop = Fblock + S(2ndV + 4d) + 2nd(T + I), = SH + 2S. (8) The term 2ndT is the content score of every block output. The term 2ndI counts the content scores of initialization writes. These comprise one write per outer cycle and two writes per segment in the carry reset. The carry reset replaces the recurrent state of puzzle that halted in the previous segment with the learned initial state. The carry reset is scored for every puzzle, because the implementation builds both the reset and the retained state before selecting one. We count the operators of one segment in the InfiLoop checkpoint and multiply by S=12. This count matches the formula at four profiled depths: 0.34, 0.92, 2.55, and 25.6 TFLOPs per puzzle at H=3, L=6, H=8, L=6, H=12, L=12, and H=32, L=48. At the depth-study setting H=6, L=12, the formula gives 1.27 TFLOPs at 1,872 layers and 17.0 TFLOPs at 24,960 layers. The content scores are the only operations of the connection in the totals above. The remaining arithmetic of the connection is elementwise. We charge each arithmetic primitive or unary function once and exclude comparisons, casts, indexing, and memory traffic. Under this convention, the remaining arithmetic adds [n(7d + 6) + 1] + In(4d + 4) scalar operations. Persistent state. The shared block attends bidirectionally over the whole input and recomputes keys and values at every application. InfiLoop keeps no KV cache between iterations. What persists between block applications is the recurrent carry. At batch size one, the two BF16 carries occupy 2nd 2 bytes, or 194.0 KiB. carry-last TRM keeps the same two carries. InfiLoop adds an FP32 numerator and denominator per position on each axis, 2n(d + 1) 4 bytes or 388.8 KiB, for total of 582.8 KiB. None of these sizes depends on H, L, or S. They scale linearly with batch size and sequence length. Model weights, input tensors, and temporary operator workspaces are not part of this accounting. B. Related Work Reasoning through recurrent depth. Universal Transformers apply one shared block repeatedly (Dehghani et al., 2019). Later work studied the computational capabilities of looped Transformers and their use for latent reasoning (Giannou et al., 14 Loop-Native Attention Residuals 2023; Saunshi et al., 2025; Geiping et al., 2025). Looped Transformers have also been studied as learners of iterative algorithms (Yang et al., 2024) and for generalization to longer input sequences (Fan et al., 2025). HRM and TRM build compact reasoners from nested latent updates (Wang et al., 2025; Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025). URM studies architecture and optimization choices for recursive reasoning (Gao et al., 2025). Adaptive Computation Time, PonderNet, and Mixture-ofRecursions learn how much computation to spend (Graves, 2016; Banino et al., 2021; Bae et al., 2025). InfiLoop modifies the connection between iterations of nested TRM-style reasoner. Overthinking in recurrent networks. Schwarzschild et al. (2021) showed that recurrent networks trained on easier problems can generalize to harder ones by taking more iterations at test time. Bansal et al. (2022) identified degradation under excessive iteration and addressed it with input recall and progressive training. Their recall connection preserves access to the original problem instance, while InfiLoop aggregates candidate states produced during reasoning. Both address behavior beyond the training iteration budget, but act on different information in the recurrence. Stabilizing deep and looped Transformers. looped Transformer at many iterations is very deep weight-shared network. Section 2 measures one consequence: carry-last TRM accuracy peaks and then falls with depth. Normalization placement affects gradient stability at initialization (Xiong et al., 2020), while depth-dependent normalization scaling controls activation growth (Sun et al., 2025). ReZero uses zero-initialized residual gate (Bachlechner et al., 2021), LayerScale learns channel-wise residual scaling (Touvron et al., 2021), and DeepNet combines residual scaling with tailored initialization (Wang et al., 2024). Residual scaling for looped Transformers controls residual growth under weight sharing (Wang et al., 2026). Deep Equilibrium Models formulate weight-tied networks through fixed-point root finding and implicit differentiation (Bai et al., 2019). FPRM combines pre-norm, learned residual scaling, and damped fixed-point updates, with convergence-based halting (Movahedi et al., 2026). Attractor Models and equilibrium reasoners use fixed-point formulations for latent reasoning (Fein-Ashley & Rashidinejad, 2026; Huang et al., 2026). At fixed point the update size is zero. These approaches stabilize recurrent computation through normalization, update scaling, or fixed-point formulations. InfiLoop instead learns from the task loss which earlier outputs the next state keeps and by how much. Learned residual connections. ResNet propagates features through identity skip connections (He et al., 2016), while DenseNet concatenates features from preceding layers (Huang et al., 2017). DenseFormer learns weights for averaging current and earlier layer outputs (Pagliardini et al., 2024). Hyper-Connections learn how to mix features across depth and parallel residual streams (Zhu et al., 2025). These works establish learned cross-layer information flow as broader design space. InfiLoop specializes this idea to shared recurrent block: content-dependent weights and exponential age decay admit running numerator and denominator whose size is independent of the number of iterations. Gated recurrent updates. The interpolation in Equation 5 has the same form as an update gate in GRU (Cho et al., 2014) or the coupled transform and carry gates in Highway Network (Srivastava et al., 2015). The distinction is the gate parameterization: γt is the ratio of the new content weight to the sum of that weight and the decayed historical mass, rather than the output of separate gating network. One shared content scorer and one decay parameter add + 1 parameters per recurrence axis. This parameterization gives the exact normalized history aggregation in Equation 2. Relation to Attention Residuals. Full Attention Residuals learns input-dependent weights over the outputs of earlier layers (Kimi Team et al., 2026). Each layer has its own pseudo-query and attends to the stored outputs of earlier layers, so memory grows with depth. blockwise variant stores block-level summaries to reduce this history. looped model has no fixed number of iterations, and loop-native connection therefore cannot store the full activation history. InfiLoop scores each output once, at its own iteration, with one scorer shared by every iteration. learned exponential decay then ages this weight. The connection keeps only running weighted sum and running normalization mass, so its memory does not grow with the loop count and the same rule applies at any depth. Retention networks also combine exponential age weighting with recurrent form (Sun et al., 2023), and ALiBi demonstrates input-length extrapolation with linear relative-position biases (Press et al., 2022). In InfiLoop, the recurrence runs over reasoning iterations and yields the next recurrent state. C. Qualitative analysis on ARC-AGI-2. Figure 6 visualizes the qualitative predictions of InfiLoop and TRM on two held-out ARC-AGI-2 evaluation tasks. In Task 5961cc34, which demands geometric expansion of spatial components, InfiLoop produces the exact target structure, while TRM produces 30 erroneous cells with distorted boundaries. In Task 80a900e0, the model must extend colored diagonal rays across an alternating checkerboard background. InfiLoop preserves the underlying background regularity while drawing sharp diagonal rays. TRM introduces 14 corrupted cells that break the checkerboard pattern and fragment the 15 Loop-Native Attention Residuals Figure 6. Qualitative comparison on ARC-AGI-2. Each row shows demonstration inputoutput pair, test input, and the predictions of InfiLoop and TRM. The top and bottom rows correspond to tasks 5961cc34 and 80a900e0, respectively. As in the pass@2 evaluation, we show the best of each models two submitted attempts. InfiLoop matches the target exactly in both cases; TRM makes 30 and 14 cell errors, respectively. rays. These qualitative results demonstrate that learned state reuse provides stability across complex spatial rules where carry-last propagation degrades structural coherence. D. Removing the Content Score Section 4.5 shows that the content score tracks board correctness. We test whether this score also matters for accuracy by removing it in two ways. Setting = 0 gives every candidate the same score si = 0, and Equation 5 then reduces the connection to an exponential moving average whose step size approaches 1 β. All results in this section use the Sudoku-Extreme test puzzles of Section 4.4, evaluated at H6 L12 with S=12, or 1,872 layers. Table 3 summarizes them. Table 3. Exact accuracy (%) on Sudoku-Extreme at H6 L12, S=12, or 1,872 layers. InfiLoop = 0 in training = 0 at test time β = 0 at test time 90.9 84.1 84.8 1.5 Removing the score during training. We train second model with the same recipe, seed, and number of training steps, and with fixed to zero on both axes. It reaches 84.1% against 90.9% for InfiLoop, so the content score is worth 6.8 percentage points when the model is trained with it. Removing the score at test time. We also set to zero in the trained InfiLoop checkpoint without retraining, and accuracy falls from 90.9% to 84.8%. Setting β to zero instead turns the connection into carry-last, and accuracy falls to 1.5%, because the block weights are trained to operate on the aggregated state rather than on raw block outputs. Both ways of removing the score lower accuracy by 6 to 7 percentage points. The gain of InfiLoop therefore does not come from damping alone: fixed exponential average also damps the updates but lacks the content score, and it is less accurate.
